record.paper_title: On some open problems of number theory
record.original_question: Let phi(n) be Euler's totient function, the number of positive integers at most n that are coprime to n. Is there an integer m for which the equation phi(x) = m has exactly one integer solution x?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$ denote Euler's totient function, defined by $\varphi(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb{Z}: 1\le k\le n,\ \gcd(k,n)=1\}$. For a positive integer $m$, let $A(m)=\#\{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}:\varphi(x)=m\}$ denote the number of preimages of $m$ under $\varphi$. Determine whether there exists a positive integer $m$ such that $A(m)=1$; that is, whether the equation $\varphi(x)=m$ has exactly one positive integer solution $x$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is Carmichael's totient function conjecture (1907), which asserts that no such $m$ exists, i.e., $A(m)\ne 1$ for every positive integer $m$. It remains a famous open problem. Ford (1998) showed that if a counterexample exists, then $m > 10^{10^{10}}$, and the bound has since been improved, but the conjecture itself is still unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Carmichael's totient function conjecture - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is conjectured that for every n there exists another m ≠ n such that φ(m) = φ(n). The conjecture remains open.
status_evidence.claim: Carmichael's conjecture (equivalent to the asked question having no such m) is still open.

status_evidence.title: Kevin Ford, The distribution of totients
status_evidence.snippet: Lower bounds on possible counterexamples to Carmichael's conjecture are obtained.
status_evidence.claim: Only lower bounds on counterexamples are known; no resolution.
